topic: Tool and MCP trust: capability discovery, per-call approval, scoped credentials, revocation, provenance, and malicious-tool containment
research_questions: How do official MCP, agent-platform, and security standards model capability discovery, trust establishment, per-call approval, and scoped credentials?
What provenance, revocation, isolation, and malicious-tool containment patterns are recommended by primary sources?
How should tool identity, capability scope, authorization evidence, and failure recovery be represented per call?
Which trust-boundary gaps matter most for Puppet Master integrations and MCP orchestration?

sources.title: Authorization - Model Context Protocol (Version 2025-11-25)
sources.material_relevance: Current MCP authorization specification for protected-resource metadata, authorization-server discovery, scope selection, resource indicators, per-request token validation, step-up authorization, and token passthrough prohibition.

sources.title: Tools - Model Context Protocol (Version 2025-06-18)
sources.material_relevance: Versioned MCP tool-discovery and invocation model, including capability declaration, tools/list, listChanged, schemas, human denial guidance, and treatment of annotations as untrusted.

sources.title: Security Best Practices - Model Context Protocol
sources.material_relevance: MCP security guidance for confused deputies, token passthrough, audience separation, SSRF, consent state, session threats, and progressive least-privilege scopes.

sources.title: Agent2Agent Protocol Specification
sources.material_relevance: Agent-platform protocol model for Agent Cards, capability and authentication discovery, optional card signatures, authenticated extended cards, per-task authorization, and task access control.

sources.title: Human-in-the-loop - OpenAI Agents SDK
sources.material_relevance: Concrete agent-platform approval model for per-call approval rules, call-ID-scoped decisions, interruptions, serialized run state, resume, and nested or handoff approvals.

sources.title: RFC 9700 - Best Current Practice for OAuth 2.0 Security
sources.material_relevance: OAuth security BCP for audience- and sender-constrained access tokens, short-lived access, refresh-token rotation, replay resistance, and resource-server validation.

sources.title: RFC 8707 - Resource Indicators for OAuth 2.0
sources.material_relevance: Defines an absolute resource parameter that lets an authorization server apply target-resource and audience restrictions to issued tokens.

sources.title: RFC 8693 - OAuth 2.0 Token Exchange
sources.material_relevance: Defines token exchange and distinguishes delegation from impersonation, including nested actor claims that preserve delegation history.

sources.title: OWASP MCP Top 10
sources.material_relevance: MCP-specific threat taxonomy for tool poisoning, rug pulls, schema poisoning, tool shadowing, supply-chain tampering, insufficient authorization, and missing audit telemetry.

sources.title: SPIFFE Workload API
sources.material_relevance: Workload-identity standard for per-process caller identification, SVID and trust-bundle delivery, streamed rotation, and rapid revocation propagation.

sources.title: SLSA Build: Track Basics (Version 1.2)
sources.material_relevance: Software supply-chain provenance levels covering builder, build process, top-level inputs, signed provenance, and the limits of unsigned or incomplete provenance.

sources.title: Security Model - gVisor
sources.material_relevance: Isolation model for untrusted code using a userspace Sentry, minimized host system-call exposure, defense in depth, and explicit network, resource, and side-channel limitations.

findings.claim: MCP capability discovery is explicit but not intrinsically trusted: servers declare the tools capability, clients enumerate tools with tools/list, servers can signal list changes, and tool annotations must be treated as untrusted unless the server is trusted.
findings.notes: The protocol supplies discovery and change-notification primitives, but the tool specification does not by itself establish publisher provenance or cryptographically bind a discovered definition to a later invocation.

findings.claim: Current MCP HTTP authorization models a protected MCP server as an OAuth resource server and requires protected-resource metadata plus authorization-server discovery before a client obtains credentials.
findings.notes: The specification separates resource-server, client, and authorization-server roles and supports pre-registration, client metadata documents, and dynamic registration according to deployment policy.

findings.claim: MCP and OAuth resource indicators provide a target-resource boundary: the client includes an absolute resource identifier in authorization and token requests, the server validates token audience, authorization is sent on every HTTP request, and MCP forbids token passthrough.
findings.notes: This is the strongest directly documented boundary against reusing an upstream credential at a different MCP or downstream resource; the downstream call should use a separately issued credential.

findings.claim: MCP uses least-privilege scope selection with runtime insufficient-scope challenges and step-up authorization; the client is expected to limit retries and track repeated scope-upgrade attempts.
findings.notes: The model separates basic discovery or read access from privilege elevation at the point the operation actually requires it, which is materially narrower than one omnibus grant.

findings.claim: A2A treats an Agent Card as a discovery contract for identity, capabilities, skills, interfaces, and authentication requirements; it supports authenticated extended cards whose contents can vary by client authorization, and it exposes TASK_STATE_AUTH_REQUIRED for in-task authorization.
findings.notes: A2A also permits JWS-signed cards and requires access checks on task operations, but card discovery remains a declaration that must be followed by transport and operation-level authorization.

findings.claim: An agent platform can model approval as a first-class per-call interruption: the OpenAI Agents SDK evaluates approval after the model emits a tool call, scopes decisions to the tool call ID by default, serializes pending state, and resumes the outer run after approval or rejection, including nested and handoff cases.
findings.notes: The SDK also supports deliberately sticky decisions, so a policy must distinguish an exact-call approval from an explicitly broader run-scoped decision.

findings.claim: OAuth security guidance recommends audience restriction and sender constraint for access tokens, short-lived access tokens, and refresh-token rotation or sender constraint for public clients to reduce replay and leakage impact.
findings.notes: Audience restriction limits where a token works; sender constraint limits who can present it. Neither replaces per-operation authorization or compromise response.

findings.claim: OAuth token exchange explicitly distinguishes delegation from impersonation and can preserve a subject plus current and prior actors through nested act claims; access control is based on the token's top-level claims and current actor, while prior actors are history.
findings.notes: This provides a standards-backed vocabulary for tool calls that travel through an orchestrator without erasing the requesting user or upstream agent.

findings.claim: SPIFFE supplies process-granular cryptographic workload identity and streams complete identity and trust-bundle updates, including SVID rotation and revocation-related changes, so consumers can replace stale material rather than merge partial state.
findings.notes: SPIFFE assumes the workload is sufficiently isolated to prevent credential theft; it does not itself solve sandboxing or application authorization policy.

findings.claim: OWASP identifies tool poisoning, rug pulls, schema poisoning, tool shadowing, supply-chain tampering, insufficient authentication and authorization, and missing audit telemetry as distinct MCP risks.
findings.notes: The taxonomy makes clear that a valid protocol connection or apparently useful tool response does not establish that the tool is safe or that its instructions should be trusted.

findings.claim: SLSA provenance can record the builder, build process, and top-level inputs; higher levels add signed provenance and stronger build-platform guarantees, while the lowest provenance level is incomplete or forgeable and therefore needs a consumer policy.
findings.notes: SLSA is useful for admission and investigation of a tool artifact, but provenance is evidence about production and not an authorization grant for runtime calls.

findings.claim: gVisor contains untrusted code behind a userspace Sentry that implements the application-facing system API and minimizes the host API surface; it still requires defense in depth, cgroup and network controls, and a secure surrounding architecture.
findings.notes: The source explicitly states that sandboxing is not a substitute for secure architecture and does not eliminate side channels or higher-level host-service vulnerabilities.

findings.claim: The standards collectively leave a compositional trust gap: discovery, artifact provenance, workload identity, per-resource credentials, model-context handling, human approval, and side-effect execution are specified by different layers rather than one end-to-end tool-call contract.
findings.notes: This is a synthesis of scope boundaries and omissions, not a claim that any one protocol is defective.

competitor_standard_patterns.pattern: Authorization-dependent discovery: expose a baseline capability description, then resolve or filter the effective tool or skill set using the authenticated principal and its scopes.
competitor_standard_patterns.implication: Capability caches should be keyed by server identity, protocol version, principal, and effective scope rather than by endpoint or connection alone.

competitor_standard_patterns.pattern: Audience- and resource-bound credentials: obtain a token for the specific resource and validate the intended audience at every protected resource boundary.
competitor_standard_patterns.implication: A Puppet Master integration should represent the target resource URI and audience validation result as authorization evidence for each call, not as global connection metadata.

competitor_standard_patterns.pattern: Progressive elevation plus explicit per-call gating: low-risk discovery can proceed with narrow scopes, while an insufficient-scope or approval decision pauses the exact operation before execution.
competitor_standard_patterns.implication: Approval should cover the resolved tool identity and exact arguments, and an authorization upgrade should not silently authorize unrelated calls.

competitor_standard_patterns.pattern: Actor-preserving delegation: downstream credentials identify the current actor while retaining the subject and delegation history rather than replacing the whole chain with an impersonated identity.
competitor_standard_patterns.implication: Call records need both effective authority and an auditable chain of who requested, delegated, approved, and executed the action.

competitor_standard_patterns.pattern: Live identity and revocation material: issue short-lived identities or credentials and propagate replacement trust material as a stream of complete updates.
competitor_standard_patterns.implication: Long-lived discovery approvals need an explicit expiry and invalidation channel; a client that misses revocation updates should fail closed for high-risk operations.

competitor_standard_patterns.pattern: Provenance-backed artifact admission: record how a tool package was built, authenticate the provenance at a stronger assurance level, and apply a consumer policy before execution.
competitor_standard_patterns.implication: A tool should be admitted by publisher, artifact digest, provenance policy, and risk tier; a signature or package name alone should not be treated as authorization.

competitor_standard_patterns.pattern: Untrusted tool content with explicit containment: treat tool metadata and returned content as data subject to trust policy, while isolating privileged execution behind server-side controls and a sandbox.
competitor_standard_patterns.implication: The model context must not be the only enforcement point; the execution boundary needs independent authorization, validation, network policy, and filesystem policy.

competitor_standard_patterns.pattern: Public versus authenticated capability views: publish non-sensitive discovery metadata, then return a richer, authorization-filtered capability view only after authentication.
competitor_standard_patterns.implication: Separate public identity and routing metadata from privileged tool or skill details, and mark which view was used for a decision.

failure_modes.failure_mode: A broad bearer token is passed through an MCP server to a downstream API or is accepted for the wrong resource, creating a confused deputy and hiding the actual caller from downstream audit logs.
failure_modes.mitigation_or_gap: Validate the inbound token audience, request a resource-bound credential for each downstream resource, never pass through the upstream token, and record the actor chain.

failure_modes.failure_mode: A cached tool or skill definition remains executable after a list change, rug pull, schema change, or authenticated capability change.
failure_modes.mitigation_or_gap: Bind approval and authorization to a version or digest of the effective definition, re-fetch on listChanged or card version change, and require re-approval for material changes.

failure_modes.failure_mode: A malicious tool uses descriptions, annotations, schemas, or returned content to inject instructions that cause the model to invoke a higher-trust tool or exfiltrate data.
failure_modes.mitigation_or_gap: Treat tool content as untrusted data, validate structured output, isolate privileged tools and contexts, enforce access server-side, and require out-of-band confirmation for sensitive effects.

failure_modes.failure_mode: Transport authentication or a valid Agent Card is mistaken for authorization to every tool, skill, task, or resource exposed by the server.
failure_modes.mitigation_or_gap: Perform operation-level authorization against the authenticated subject, actor, target resource, tool or skill, input attributes, and current scopes; do not treat discovery claims as grants.

failure_modes.failure_mode: Delegation drops the original subject or actor lineage, allowing a lower-trust orchestrator to wield a higher-privilege credential without a reviewable chain.
failure_modes.mitigation_or_gap: Use token exchange or an equivalent envelope that preserves subject and current actor, constrain delegated scope and audience, and deny calls when lineage or delegation purpose is missing.

failure_modes.failure_mode: A revoked or rotated workload identity, signing key, trust bundle, or credential remains in a local cache because the consumer missed an update or merged partial state.
failure_modes.mitigation_or_gap: Use short validity, complete replacement updates, reconnect and resynchronize after stream loss, track freshness, and fail closed for high-impact calls when revocation state is stale.

failure_modes.failure_mode: A tool package with weak, unsigned, incomplete, or unverified provenance is admitted because identity or a signature is treated as proof that the artifact is trustworthy.
failure_modes.mitigation_or_gap: Require a consumer policy over publisher identity, artifact digest, builder and source provenance, dependency posture, and risk tier; distinguish provenance evidence from runtime authorization.

failure_modes.failure_mode: An untrusted local tool executes with host filesystem, credential, network, or process privileges, and sandboxing is assumed to cover resource exhaustion, higher-level service flaws, or hardware side channels.
failure_modes.mitigation_or_gap: Use defense-in-depth isolation, least-privilege mounts and credentials, cgroup and network policy, and a sandbox tier appropriate to the tool's risk; retain host and service hardening.

failure_modes.failure_mode: An approval intended for one call is replayed or widened to a different call, or a sticky approval outlives the definition, arguments, identity, or risk context it was meant to cover.
failure_modes.mitigation_or_gap: Default to exact call-ID, tool-definition digest, argument digest, principal, and expiry binding; require an explicit policy for any run-wide always-approve decision.

failure_modes.failure_mode: A non-idempotent side effect is repeated after an authorization challenge, connection loss, or ambiguous timeout because the retry path cannot distinguish a rejected, unexecuted, or already executed call.
failure_modes.mitigation_or_gap: Use explicit call states, idempotency keys where supported, bounded retries only for safe classes, and a reconciliation or user-confirmation path for ambiguous side effects.

implications.implication: Represent discovered tools as expiring capability leases rather than permanent registrations.
implications.rationale: MCP and A2A both allow capability views to change, while OAuth and SPIFFE provide short-lived or refreshed trust material. A lease can carry definition version, principal, scopes, freshness, and expiry in one revocable unit.

implications.implication: Every tool call needs an authorization-evidence envelope independent of the model's tool-call JSON.
implications.rationale: The model emits a name and arguments, but resource audience, scopes, subject, actor chain, approval, freshness, and policy decision are established outside the model context and must be carried to the executor.

implications.implication: A call should be authorized against a digest of the effective tool definition and normalized arguments, not just a tool name.
implications.rationale: Tool poisoning and rug pulls target definitions, while per-call approval targets arguments. Binding both prevents a later schema or argument substitution from inheriting an earlier decision.

implications.implication: Downstream integrations should use resource-specific token exchange or equivalent credential issuance rather than forwarding the credential that arrived at the orchestrator.
implications.rationale: Audience restriction, delegation semantics, and the MCP token-passthrough prohibition all point to separate downstream authorization contexts with preserved lineage.

implications.implication: Revocation must be a control-plane event that invalidates cached leases, credentials, tool definitions, and trust keys, not only a periodic audit observation.
implications.rationale: SPIFFE demonstrates streaming identity replacement and OAuth describes rotation and revocation responses; Puppet Master needs one integration-level invalidation path across all cached trust decisions.

implications.implication: Tool results should enter model context through a typed, provenance-aware data channel with explicit untrusted status, while privileged actions remain behind an execution gate.
implications.rationale: MCP flags untrusted annotations and OWASP describes contextual payloads and tool poisoning; neither supports treating arbitrary tool output as trusted instructions.

implications.implication: Local or third-party tools should be assigned an isolation tier based on reachable data, side effects, and credential exposure, with sandbox, network, filesystem, and process policy enforced outside the model.
implications.rationale: gVisor supplies a containment pattern but explicitly requires surrounding controls; OWASP identifies sandbox escapes and over-privileged servers as MCP risks.

implications.implication: Admission evidence should include artifact digest, publisher, builder or source provenance, runtime workload identity, and the policy decision that accepted the tool.
implications.rationale: SLSA covers production history and SPIFFE covers runtime identity; together they support a stronger admission record than a package name or protocol handshake.

implications.implication: Audit events should preserve subject, current actor, delegation history, resource audience, scope, tool-definition digest, argument digest, approval decision, credential version, outcome, and retry state.
implications.rationale: This joins the identity, authorization, approval, and telemetry fields that the cited sources address separately and makes incident reconstruction possible without trusting model narration.

implications.implication: Recovery should classify authorization, trust freshness, definition change, transport, and side-effect ambiguity separately; blind retry is not a safe universal recovery policy.
implications.rationale: The sources provide distinct 401, 403, authorization-required, stream-refresh, and task-state concepts; a single retry loop would erase those safety distinctions.

novel_ideas.idea: Capability lease tuple: store server identity, canonical endpoint, protocol version, tool or skill definition digest, principal, scope set, artifact digest, trust tier, observed-at, expires-at, and invalidation generation as one lease.
novel_ideas.rationale: It unifies authorization-dependent discovery, definition-change detection, credential freshness, and revocation into an object that can be invalidated before execution.

novel_ideas.idea: Two-phase call gate: let the model propose a call, then have a non-model executor re-resolve the lease, policy, fresh credential, actor chain, and human approval against an immutable call hash immediately before side effects.
novel_ideas.rationale: The model-call surface and the execution authority are different trust domains; re-resolution closes the time-of-check/time-of-use gap created by changing scopes, definitions, or revocation state.

novel_ideas.idea: Authorization evidence envelope: carry subject, current actor, prior actors, target resource URI, effective scopes, tool-definition digest, normalized-argument digest, approval reference, credential fingerprint, expiry, nonce, and policy result alongside the call.
novel_ideas.rationale: The envelope makes per-call authorization inspectable and prevents the executor from inferring authority from an untrusted natural-language transcript.

novel_ideas.idea: Poison-aware context broker: classify every tool description, schema, annotation, and result as untrusted or trusted-by-policy, validate typed fields, retain provenance, and expose instructions to the model only through a marked data channel.
novel_ideas.rationale: This treats model-context contamination as a separate trust boundary from network authorization and gives Puppet Master a place to quarantine suspicious content without pretending that prompt filtering is complete.

novel_ideas.idea: Provenance-to-isolation admission matrix: map artifact provenance assurance, publisher policy, runtime identity, requested scopes, and side-effect risk to a required sandbox and approval tier.
novel_ideas.rationale: A tool with good build provenance can still be over-privileged or compromised at runtime; joining provenance with isolation and call-risk policy avoids a binary trusted/untrusted decision.

novel_ideas.idea: Revocation generation fence: assign a monotonically increasing generation to each server, identity domain, credential family, and tool-definition lineage; a call is rejected when its evidence was minted before the current fence.
novel_ideas.rationale: Complete replacement updates and change notifications provide the inputs; a generation fence turns them into a cheap, deterministic stale-evidence check across caches.

unresolved_questions.question: Which interoperable field, if any, binds a particular MCP tool-definition digest and normalized argument digest to the access-token or approval evidence for one call?
What common revocation signal and freshness service should invalidate MCP capability caches, A2A Agent Cards, OAuth credentials, and workload identities across protocol boundaries?
How should Puppet Master combine package provenance, publisher policy, runtime workload identity, live server state, and risk classification into one admission decision for a newly discovered tool?
What validation boundary and failure semantics are sufficient to prevent malicious tool outputs from becoming executable model instructions without blocking legitimate structured data?
How should approval authority, delegation history, and scope changes compose when a tool call crosses nested agents, MCP servers, and downstream services?
What interoperable idempotency, reconciliation, and rollback contract should govern non-idempotent tool effects after an authorization challenge, timeout, disconnect, or ambiguous response?
For local stdio MCP servers, what portable workload identity and scoped-credential mechanism should replace environment-provided credentials when the tool needs per-process trust and revocation?
